title: How 3D Printing Works
summary: Josh Clark opens with an unusual intro: Chuck Bryant is absent, and Ben Boldin sits in as co-host. After a dream-themed tangent, the hosts explain 3D printing (additive manufacturing) as layer-by-layer construction. They cover its history (rapid prototyping in the mid-1980s, Charles Hull's stereolithography and 3D Systems), the main processes (direct/extrusion printing, binder jetting, multi-jet modeling, fused deposition modeling, selective laser sintering), the CAD-to-STL workflow and printing steps, and applications in industry, medicine, dental work, art, commerce, home inventing, the open-source RepRap and Mendel printers, and 3D-printed food. They also discuss downsides (energy use, emissions, plastics), intellectual property piracy, and 3D-printed guns. The episode closes with listener mail about wild parrots and a sign-off.

segments.title: Chuck's absence and Ben Boldin's debut; dream tangent
segments.summary: Josh announces that Chuck Bryant has been called away and Ben Boldin is sitting in as co-host. The hosts joke about Josh's dream that the show went on without him, then set up the 3D printing topic.

segments.title: What 3D printing is; additive manufacturing
segments.summary: The hosts introduce 3D printing as additive manufacturing, building objects layer by layer, contrasting it with CNC machining from a block. They discuss the range of objects that can be made and speculate about it as a possible new industrial revolution, including custom home-made items.

segments.title: History: rapid prototyping and stereolithography
segments.summary: The hosts describe 3D printing's introduction to industry in the mid-1980s as rapid prototyping, which shortened prototype cycles. They credit MIT and several parallel efforts, note car companies as early buyers, and describe Charles Hull's laser-based photopolymerization technique and his company 3D Systems.

segments.title: Direct, binder, multi-jet and fused deposition printing
segments.summary: The hosts explain direct 3D printing, which extrudes melted plastic or wax like a hot glue gun, and binder printing, which spreads powder and sprays a liquid binder. They also cover multi-jet modeling and fused deposition modeling, and predict that one technology will become the consumer standard, as inkjet did.

segments.title: Laser-based methods and why layered printing matters
segments.summary: The hosts discuss using UV lasers and selective laser sintering for powders and metals. They explain that printed objects can be hollow or lattice-structured, reducing material waste and weight, with the airplane hinge example.
